title: How to Build an IB English Study Group This Fall
summary: Build an IB English study group for September-November with clear roles, focused agendas, Paper 1 and Paper 2 practice, and accountability.
body_markdown:
An **IB English study group** works when every meeting produces something assessable: an essay plan, analytical paragraph, comparison grid, or recorded oral rehearsal. For the September-November term, aim for **3-5 reliable members** , meet weekly for 60-75 minutes, and organize each session around one precise skill.


The group should support independent thinking, not replace it. IB English assessments require each student to interpret texts, construct arguments, and communicate clearly on their own.


### Start with the assessment, not the friendship group


Choose members based on reliability, compatible schedules, and willingness to receive criticism. Friends can work well together if they can stop social conversation when timed work begins.


At the first meeting, establish which English course and level everyone takes. In **English A: Language and Literature** , Paper 1 examines unseen non-literary texts; in **English A: Literature** , it examines unseen literary passages. Both courses include a comparative Paper 2, while the texts used for the Individual Oral differ.


Official IB subject briefs emphasize interpreting texts, analysing authorial choices, evaluating relationships between texts, and communicating persuasively. Shared summaries alone cannot develop these skills.


Record:


- Each member's course and level
- Texts studied in class
- Teacher deadlines and planned assessments
- Individual weaknesses, such as organization, close analysis, comparison, or oral delivery
- One measurable group target for the end of November


### Agree on rules that protect working time


Write a short agreement before the second meeting. These are recommendations, not official IB rules.


- Arrive with the assigned text read and annotated.
- Complete individual work before comparing answers.
- Keep phones away unless used as timers or recording devices.
- Critique the writing, not the writer.
- Do not write assessed coursework for another member.
- Notify the group early if you cannot attend.
- End every meeting by assigning the next task.


Rotate four roles: **facilitator** , **timekeeper** , **discussion challenger** , and **scribe** . The challenger asks, “What precise authorial choice supports that interpretation?” The scribe records conclusions and recurring errors without creating complete notes for absent members.


See RevisionDojo's[IB study group revision strategies](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/strategies-for-revising-with-study-groups-in-ib) for additional guidance on roles and focused practice.


### Use a repeatable 70-minute meeting structure


Time Activity Required output


0-5 minutes Set the question and assign roles One written session goal


5-20 minutes Silent individual task Annotation, thesis, or plan


20-35 minutes Compare interpretations Two supported similarities or disagreements


35-55 minutes Timed writing or oral practice One paragraph or recorded response


55-65 minutes Criterion-based feedback One strength and one priority improvement


65-70 minutes Log errors and assign preparation Named task and deadline for each member


Silent work prevents confident speakers from shaping everyone else's interpretation. Independent analysis gives the group several readings to evaluate and rehearses assessment conditions.


Keep a shared error log with four categories: **interpretation** , **analysis** , **organization** , and **language** . Express errors as actionable rules, such as “Explain how the contrast changes the audience's view,” rather than “analysis was weak.”


### Follow a September-November study plan


### September: establish analytical routines


Practise identifying patterns in diction, imagery, tone, structure, narrative perspective, and visual design where relevant. Each week, annotate an unfamiliar extract independently, propose a thesis, compare approaches, and write one analytical paragraph.


RevisionDojo's[English study techniques guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/effective-study-techniques-for-ib-english-a-language-and-literature) and[Paper 1 Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-english-langlit-new/ib-english-langlit-new-2-paper-1/questionbank) provide common practice material.


### October: strengthen comparison and evidence retrieval


For each Paper 2 pair, build a grid covering themes, authorial choices, significant moments, contextual considerations, and differences in effect. Do not assign one work to each member because everyone must retrieve evidence from both works independently.


Use the official[Paper 2 specimen paper](https://ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/dp/pdfs/english-a-literature-hl-sl-paper-2-en.pdf) to practise interpreting questions, then consult RevisionDojo's guide to[studying for Paper 1 and Paper 2](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-s-the-best-way-to-study-for-paper-1-vs-paper-2) .


### November: introduce time pressure


Alternate between Paper 1 planning, Paper 2 comparative outlines, and oral rehearsals according to your class schedule. During oral practice, one student speaks, another keeps time, and the others record questions.


Feedback should address the global issue, relationship between extract and wider work, analysis of authorial choices, and organization. The[RevisionDojo Individual Oral guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/comprehensive-guide-to-the-ib-individual-oral-io-for-language-and-literature-and-literature) offers a fuller rehearsal framework.


### Give feedback that changes the next attempt


Use a three-part feedback formula:


1. **Locate:** Identify the exact sentence or moment.
2. **Diagnose:** Explain what is effective or missing.
3. **Direct:** Suggest the next action without rewriting the response.


For example: “Your second paragraph identifies repetition, but it does not explain the changing effect. Trace how the repeated word becomes more threatening across the passage.” This preserves the writer's ownership while setting a concrete revision task.


Ask members to rewrite one paragraph after feedback. Short revision cycles make improvement visible and manageable. RevisionDojo's[IB English note-taking strategies](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/effective-note-taking-strategies-for-ib-english-language-and-literature) can help convert feedback into comparison grids, technique notes, and self-testing prompts.


### Avoid unproductive habits


Replace a vague agenda such as “review the novel” with an observable result: “Create two comparative claims about how both authors present authority, supported by one method and one moment from each work.”


Avoid:


- Rereading material that should have been prepared beforehand
- Sharing quotations without analysing how they create meaning
- Allowing one student to supply every interpretation
- Correcting grammar while ignoring argument and analysis
- Writing collaborative paragraphs nobody can reproduce independently
- Giving feedback without requiring revision


Protect academic integrity. Students may discuss interpretations and offer feedback, but they must follow school rules and submit their own work. For the Higher Level Essay and other assessed tasks, question reasoning rather than composing or rewriting another student's response.


### Conclusion


An effective **IB English study group** is small, scheduled, assessment-focused, and built around individual output. From September through November, progress from analytical routines to comparative thinking and then timed writing or oral rehearsal.


Keep a shared agenda and error log while requiring independent work. RevisionDojo can support this cycle with Study Notes, Flashcards, the Questionbank, and Jojo AI for testing interpretations and generating follow-up questions.
